raw_response.country: Multiple low- and middle-income countries (Argentina, India, and South Africa explicitly named in the provided main text; additional LMIC study settings in truncated study tables)

criterion_notes.c1: Yes. Although the review broadly evaluates physical slum upgrading on health and socio-economic wellbeing, water and sanitation infrastructure improvements (piped water connections, public taps, latrines, sewerage, and drainage) are core components of the interventions studied, and the review also examines household water expenditure/affordability, connection fidelity, and resident perspectives on water and sanitation service use.
criterion_notes.c2: No under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading; Yes under the plain/broad wording (plain=yes, narrow=no). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the review passes because it examines state/municipal, NGO, community-managed, and privatised slum-upgrading delivery programmes (including privatised water connection expansion in Galiani 2007, multicomponent packages bundling land tenure or eviction guarantees, community engagement comparisons, and qualitative observations on user-fee non-payment closing public taps in Milone 1993 and state land acquisition impairing maintenance in Moitra 1987). Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification, however, Criterion 2 fails: the mandatory exposure across all included studies is generic physical environment and infrastructure project delivery (installing water pipes, toilets, drains, paved roads, or cement floors vs. unupgraded slums), optional legal/tenure co-interventions are bundled into unisolated multicomponent packages evaluated for health/income effects rather than tested as rules governing service access, and external policy/governance contexts are unanalysed background with insufficient detail to draw conclusions.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. This is a Cochrane systematic empirical synthesis screening 10,488 unique records and synthesizing 14 empirical primary studies (5 main experimental/quasi-experimental studies: 1 cluster-RCT and 4 cluster-CBAs; plus 9 supporting UBA and CPI studies).
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. While most synthesized outcomes are health (diarrhoea, parasitic infections, mortality) and general socio-economic indicators (income, employment, literacy), the review explicitly prespecifies 'time or proportion of income spent on water or fuel collection' under financial poverty and reports quantitative water-affordability outcomes (monthly water-related expenditure in Galiani 2007 and Aiga 2002; mean proportion of household income spent on water in Aiga 2002), alongside fidelity/process and qualitative evidence on water/sewerage connection coverage (Soares 2005; Joshi 2002; Abelson 1996), waiting times at public faucets (Aiga 2002), and public tap shutoffs due to unpaid fees (Milone 1993).
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population (urban/peri-urban slum dwellers in LMICs; household, individual, and cluster/settlement units noted), exposure (in situ physical environment and infrastructure slum upgrading), outcomes, and study design (Cochrane systematic review of RCT, CBA, CPI, and UBA studies) are clearly identified in the 40 pages of main text provided.

evidence_quotes.quote: We included studies examining the impact of slum upgrading strategies involving physical environment or infrastructure improvements (with or without additional co-interventions) on the health, quality of life and socio-economic wellbeing of LMIC urban slum dwellers.

The review examined slum upgrading programmes involving at least one or more physical environment or infrastructure change to the slum environment in situ; with or without the inclusion of policy, financial, legal, behavioural, educational, social environment, or health and social service interventions.
Limited information was available in the eligible studies on the policy and planning environment that the implemented slum upgrading interventions were operating within.
Due to the limitations of the available evidence described above, it was not possible to draw conclusions on whether particular intervention actors boost or hinder programme delivery and outcomes.
On completion of the selection process 21 publications reporting five main studies and nine supporting studies were included.

The multicomponent slum upgrading programme evaluated by Soares 2005 was found to significantly increase access to sewerage, water and rubbish collection, though it was not reported whether this achieved full access to all participants surveyed.

Mean water expenditure and mean proportion of income spent on water was lower in the intervention group who received improved water supply as part of multicomponent slum upgrading, than the control group (109 peso/household/months in the intervention slum compared to 234 peso/household/month in control slum, P < 0.01; and 2.8% in the intervention slum compared to 10.1% in the control slum, P < 0.05, respectively) (Aiga 2002).

raw_response.exposure: In situ slum upgrading strategies involving at least one physical environment or infrastructure intervention (piped water supply, sanitation/latrines, drainage/sewerage, road paving, cement flooring, waste collection), delivered alone or in multicomponent packages alongside optional health, social, financial, or land-tenure co-interventions
raw_response.outcome: Primary: health and quality of life (communicable diseases such as diarrhoea and parasitic infections, infant and sanitation-related mortality, nutritional deficiencies, mental health, homicides, life satisfaction). Secondary: socio-economic outcomes including monthly water-related expenditure and share of household income spent on water (affordability), household income, poverty headcount, employment, education, crime, social capital, plus intervention fidelity (water/sewerage access) and resident perspectives on facility siting, fees, and time saved
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban and peri-urban slum dwellers in low- and middle-income countries across 14 included studies (21 publications): 5 main studies (3,453 households or observations across 4 studies reporting sample sizes; 1 study sample size unclear) and 9 supporting studies (6,794 households or observations across 8 studies reporting sample sizes; 1 study sample size not reported)
raw_response.rationale: This Cochrane systematic review (Turley et al., 2013) synthesizes 5 main studies (1 cluster-RCT, 4 cluster-CBAs) and 9 supporting studies (6 CPIs, 3 UBAs) evaluating in situ slum upgrading programmes involving physical environment and infrastructure improvements in LMIC urban slums. Although the review primarily focuses on health and general socio-economic outcomes, it explicitly prespecifies and reports water-affordability outcomes (monthly water expenditure and share of household income spent on water in Galiani 2007 and Aiga 2002) as well as process/fidelity and qualitative findings on water/sanitation connection coverage and fee-related public tap shutoffs, satisfying c1, c3, and c4. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): the required intervention is generic physical infrastructure project delivery (installing water connections, latrines, drains, road paving, or cement floors vs. no intervention), optional legal/tenure co-components in multicomponent upgrading packages are not isolated or evaluated as rules governing water/sanitation access, and institutional/governance contexts remain unanalysed background. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because municipal, privatised, and community-managed upgrading delivery arrangements and bundled tenure packages constitute broad institutional/governance interventions.
raw_response.study_design: Systematic review (Cochrane intervention review with narrative synthesis and harvest plots of 1 cluster-RCT, 4 cluster-CBAs, 6 controlled post-intervention studies, and 3 uncontrolled before-and-after studies)
